title: Owner contributions and draws in the books

sections.skill: Record owner contributions, draws and loans without distorting profit

questions.prompt: An owner puts 1,000 dollars into the business. Is it sales revenue?

choices.text: Yes, but only if it is spent the same day
No, it is a business expense instead
Yes, it counts as sales for that month
No, it is an owner contribution

questions.correct_answer: No, it is an owner contribution
questions.intro: In the books, owner money is kept separate from income and expenses. An OWNER CONTRIBUTION increases the owner's stake (called owner's equity) but is NOT sales revenue. An OWNER DRAW decreases owner's equity but is NOT a business expense for a sole proprietor or most LLCs. A LOAN from the owner is recorded as money the business owes back. Mislabeling these makes profit look wrong: a contribution recorded as a sale inflates profit; a draw recorded as an expense hides it.

sections.skill: Money moving in the family versus money from customers

questions.prompt: Grandma's loan to the bakery is what?

choices.text: Family money moving in, not a sale
A flour expense for the cakes

questions.correct_answer: Family money moving in, not a sale
questions.intro: Picture a family bakery. When Grandma lends the bakery money, that is family money moving in, not a cake sale. When the baker takes money home, that is family money moving out, not the cost of flour. Only cake sales are revenue, and only business costs like flour are expenses. Mixing family moves with sales and costs gives a false picture of how the bakery is doing.

questions.prompt: The baker taking money home is what?

choices.text: Family money moving out, not an expense
The cost of flour for the week's cakes

questions.correct_answer: Family money moving out, not an expense
